strengths: The paper addresses a useful problem with an identifiable audience in program analysis and code representation learning. Aligning LLVM IR with source code and comments could provide useful representations without requiring those additional modalities at inference time.
The combination of frozen source/comment encoders, contrastive alignment, and learned interpolation is a plausible approach. The framework overview communicates the main idea effectively.

The reported results provide promising empirical signals across several tasks. Function-name accuracy improves from 29.41 to 33.41, and summarization BLEU-4 improves from GraphCodeBERT’s 32.43 to 34.36.

The paper includes component ablations, a comment-source comparison, a negative example, and an extension to CodeT5. Dataset statistics, fine-tuning settings, and a reported public release of code, models, and data are useful reproducibility resources.
weaknesses: Necessary: Resolve the evaluation-protocol inconsistencies. Section 2.3 describes supervised cross-entropy classification, while Section 3.2 and Table 2 give POJ-104 disjoint training/development/test label sets of 64/16/24 problems. Section 4.2 nevertheless describes classification and reporting across all 104 classes. Explain whether the experiment actually measures retrieval or classification, including the prediction procedure and metric definitions. Also reconcile Section 3.2’s validation-set evaluation for AnghaBench generation with Section 4.3’s test-set description and clarify how evaluation data are separated from model selection.

Necessary: Match the binary-analysis claims to the evaluated inputs. The experiments use compiler-emitted LLVM IR, and the generation examples retain informative function, callee, and type names. This does not establish performance on stripped native executables. The footnote claiming these representations are trivially interchangeable is inaccurate. Either narrow the conclusions to the evaluated LLVM IR setting and document retained information, or provide evidence using representations recovered from stripped binaries.

Necessary: The interpolation ablation does not isolate the claimed mechanism. Sections 3.1 and 5.1 compare 10-epoch primary-only training with 30-epoch full training for analysis tasks; the training stages also use different losses. Consequently, Table 7’s improvement cannot be attributed specifically to interpolation or the gradual schedule. A comparison controlling training duration and objective is needed to retain that attribution; otherwise, describe the result as a comparison between complete training recipes.

Necessary: Narrow or substantiate the human-versus-generated comment conclusion. Table 7 reports a striking MAP collapse from 43.78 to 3.11 with human comments, but removing comments yields 42.76. Thus, the evidence suggests a severe problem with the tested human-comment condition and a comparatively small benefit from generated comments. It does not establish that verbosity, implementation detail, or human authorship causes the collapse. Document extraction, filtering, missing-comment handling, and whether examples and training settings are matched; restrict generalizations unless these explanations are tested.

Necessary: The generation evaluation supports lexical reconstruction more directly than semantic correctness. BLEU, GLEU, ROUGE, exact match, and selected examples do not establish the broad claims about semantic consistency and practical reverse engineering. Compilation or behavioral checks for generated code, and an independent assessment of summary correctness, would support those claims. Alternatively, explicitly limit the conclusions to the measured reconstruction outcomes.

Necessary: Calibrate claims of significant and consistent superiority. Results use single seeds without uncertainty estimates. In Table 6, ContraBin has lower BLEU than GraphCodeBERT, while its GLEU and exact-match advantages are only 0.53 and 0.43 points. Provide uncertainty for the comparisons supporting the main conclusions or remove unsupported significance and robustness language. The mixed reverse-engineering result should also be reflected in the abstract and conclusion.

Necessary: Make the implemented training procedure unambiguous. The text and Algorithm 1 allow selecting arbitrary modality pairs, whereas other descriptions use frozen source/comment representations against the trainable binary encoder. Figure 3 concatenates embeddings, while Equations 8 and 10 add them. Specify the actual pairing rules, interpolation-network inputs, and gradient flow, including whether the model-dependent targets in Equation 5 are detached. These details affect reproduction of the central method.
Optional: Quantitative neighborhood analysis would strengthen the qualitative embedding discussion. Reducing repeated human-learning analogies would also make the technical presentation more concise.
